See also Non-physical shading: access to lighting within the fragment() function https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/1620

I think it looks great. Simple but solves a lot of the issues shader authors have run into related to composing data from multiple lights, as well as enabling shader authors to override fog behavior after lighting.

There is work to allow the whole scene shader to be overridden, but given how simple this change is, I think it makes sense even in cases where you might not want to replace the whole scene shader

That said, this would need consensus with the rendering team, and given the tight release schedule, I'm not sure how many rendering meetings there are between now and feature freeze for 4.6, so it might end up in 4.7 if it's too tight. I'd recommend you attend the next rendering meeting and add this to the agenda (godot team meetings are public. Rendering schedule is once per week alternating morning and evening times. Check the calendar)

> See also Non-physical shading: access to lighting within the fragment() function [godotengine/godot-proposals#1620](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/1620)

I would say this PR should be able to alleviate many limitations described there in practice, but does not close this issue.

This PR offers the ability to do post-lighting composition, and provides access to post-decal surface properties and fog information. In common NPR workflow, I am confident that this should be enough to meet most requirements. However, more advanced logic such as non-standard decal influence aggregation, customized shadowmap sampling and filtering, are out of the scope of this PR, but are relevant to that proposal.

> There is work to allow the whole scene shader to be overridden, but given how simple this change is, I think it makes sense even in cases where you might not want to replace the whole scene shader

Yes, I am aware of that. My opinion is similar to yours: this PR aims to provide an easy to use feature to address limitations commonly found in NPR pipelines.

For advanced NPR effects (and some PBR effects, too), more intrusive modifications are required, and they would quickly become a headache for maintainers if we are trying to expose all sort of things to gdshader, while trying to maintain compatibility across renderers. A GLSL-level override would single-handedly rule them all without added architectural complexity.

That proposal(s) and features, however, require in-depth knowledge to the rendering process from the user side, and are a bit overkill for some common techniques, imho. So this PR tries to provide features with a higher level of abstraction, balancing usability and capability, providing a better out-of-the box experience for engine users. And its modifications are minimal - this PR simply wrapped the vanilla logic into #ifdefs and registered some additional variables in the shader compiler. I would expect it to have minimal overhead of maintenance and performance (it should be free if not used, and mostly trivial when enabled).

> That said, this would need consensus with the rendering team, and given the tight release schedule, I'm not sure how many rendering meetings there are between now and feature freeze for 4.6, so it might end up in 4.7 if it's too tight. I'd recommend you attend the next rendering meeting and add this to the agenda (godot team meetings are public. Rendering schedule is once per week alternating morning and evening times. Check the calendar)

According to my discussions with the rendering team, they're not quite willing to merge this because it introduces an obvious feature disparity between the compatibility renderer vs. the other 2 renderers. Namely, it does not work as one may expect when using compatibility renderer AND light source with shadow enabled.

The reasoning about why this might be acceptable in the 1st comment is my own argument, and the rendering team (understandably) doesn't seem to agree with that.

If we are to eliminate this feature disparity, we would need to do some non-trivial work to the compatibility renderer. The issue here is that the comp. renderer renders shadowed lights in separate passes:

In the other 2 renderers, shadow map textures of multiple lights are stitched into a single atlas texture, and the information about which light is mapped to which region in the atlas is communicated to the shader via some (uniform or similar) buffers. The fragment shader of the object then simply run a loop to process all the lights. In this case, info about all the lights are aggregated before compose() runs.

However, the compatibility renderer only does this when lights are shadowless - the for loop is only responsible for shadowless lights, all shadowed lights are processed in separate passes, one pass for each light. And there's not real shadow atlas, each light has its own shadow texture, which are collectively organized as a "virtual texture atlas" in the C++ layer. So the compose() function could only get info about shadowless lights.

Actually, any light aggregation logic other than additive in light() is already broken without this PR, as the output of light passes is added to the base image. compose() seems to be (arguably) a more obvious broken thing when it comes to the comp. renderer, I guess.

To fully support the comp. renderer, a 1-pass rendering routine must be implemented (resolving [proposal#8050](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8050)). Based on what I have seen in the code, implementing a real shadow atlas (or rather re-implementing? I think there was indeed a shadow atlas implementation in Godot 3 with GLES renderer) is likely a must. You cannot really use e.g., arrays of samplers to implement 1-pass shadowed lights, especially with GLES, where things like # of samplers are often highly constrained. This is not something that can be done trivially, and I think it, by itself, does not quite worth the effort. I'd appreciate it if anyone is willing to tackle that, but I would advice everyone to thoroughly evaluate its potential complexity before starting (unless you have a very smart idea of implementing it, of course).

Speaking about the feature of this PR itself, it should be fairly stable, I think. I am currently using it in production project. Good news is that Godot is easy to compile, and this PR is easy to cherry-pick. For people really interested in this feature for their projects, I suggest trying to use a custom build of Godot (refer to the [doc](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/engine_details/development/compiling/index.html) for reference). I also made patched branches of 4.5 stable and 4.6 stable on the [npr-4.5](https://github.com/HEX-23/godot-NPR/tree/npr-4.5) & [npr-4.6](https://github.com/HEX-23/godot-NPR/tree/npr-4.6) branches of [this fork](https://github.com/HEX-23/godot-NPR). Note that there might be additional features there.

(I think [proposal#4287](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4287) implies it might be possible to replace the renderer using GDExtension). I think this is not doable at the moment, and probably not the best idea even when it is supported.

### The GDExtension side

The GDExtension system is, rather than a mechanism that exposes the real C-level API, a scripting API. From my own experience with it I would say that its principle is, in a nutshell:

- Godot registers some of its classes via ClassDB (a runtime registry of type information), each of them is exposing some explicitly chosen interface.
- These infos are used to wire things up to GDScript and C#. GDExtension is simply communicating with ClassDB with a C-level API. It only has access to what have been exposed in the ClassDB, just like GDScript and C#.
- The primary advantage of GDExtension is that it allows implementing custom logic in arbitrary languages that be compiled to dynamic libs, without actually recompiling / statically linking to the engine itself.

Specifically, for Godot CPP, you will notice that aside from grabbing the godot-cpp repo, you also need to dump an API file from the godot executable, and then build godot-cpp with that API file.

This generated API file contains information about everything exposed to GDScript, or in general, the scripting layer. This includes the names of all the classes visible to scripting languages, the interface of their methods, etc.

Under the hood, at build time, godot-cpp uses python to perform code generation (or meta programming, if you prefer that name) based on the API file. It first generates a bunch of files containing C++ classes with the specified interfaces and build them to produce a static lib. If you peek into the generated code (the definitions part), you will notice that almost all of the methods are simply implemented as:

- Queries and stores a handle / pointer object to the real implementation of that method statically (on first invocation)
- Submit the parameters as an array of variants, and ask godot to call that function, cast the returned value if needed.

These are all "dummy" classes, they have 0 binary relationship with the underlying C++ types of the engine. They are merely a set of convenient interfaces that encapsulates the tedious and error-prone C-level GDExtension API. I would say this is a clever design that maximizes compatibility no matter what compiler tool chain and engine version are you using, at the cost of a mostly forgettable runtime performance drop.

Anyway, the key takeaway here is that GDExtensions are essentially part of the scripting system, and are only capable of accessing what is being exposed to them.

### The PR side

Godot uses its own shading language in non-RD shaders. Although it sometimes seems to be like a simple preprocessor, to support proper highlight and completion (aka a Language Server) and the enforcement of a complete set of well-defined rules, it is actually implemented as a real compiler (or transpiler), just that its backend is generating GLSL fragments.

Modifications introduced by this PR is, technically:

- Register a new entrypoint function to the compiler, along with a bunch of built-in variables (their types, and the mapping between their in-GDShader name and their in-GLSL name).
- Lift the restriction on varying assignment in the shader compiler / checker.
- Prepare injection point for the generated GLSL code in some "shader template file" with preprocessing directives, ensures that built-in logics are gracefully replaced when a compose() function is in play.

If you know what this system is doing, the changes needed are actually quite simple. And you automatically get semantic highlight and auto completion, etc.

Unfortunately, the whole GDShader compiler thing is purely internal to the engine, and are not visible to the ClassDB. Not to mention that shader template file, which is baked directly into the engine binary as constant strings. These things are not easily modifiable without recompiling the engine.

While it is possible to construct graphics pipeline with the current RD interface, hacking the scene renderer itself is not something that can be done trivially.

> I think [proposal#4287](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/4287) implies it might be possible to replace the renderer using GDExtension

From what I have read in that PR, it is about some more sophisticated changes to the renderer. And even when that is made possible, I think it is way too overkill to implement a whole renderer just for a new injection point in the core shader - writing a working, modern renderer is absolutely no joke.

### Other Possibilities

I suggest checking out [PR#11939](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/111939) if you are interested in the idea of "making plugin-like things to enable the compose() function". It implemented a way to replace the core shader (the template into which compiled GDShader entry functions are injected) for a specific renderer.

It is fairly "bare-bones" at the moment, it has rough corners, and it doesn't allow very sophisticated customizations such as adding new entry point functions (so you have to implement compose() or similar functions directly in GLSL, without all the auto completion goodies, etc.). But a follow-up PR should be reasonably easy to make once it is merged. Since it targets specific renderer from the start and is targeting users with slightly more advanced knowledge about the rendering pipeline, it avoided the "feature disparity between renderers" issue and is more likely to get merged.

Hi, we are planning to use this PR in an upcoming game, since we don't care about the compatibility renderer. I found an issue with the way the ambient light is passed to the compose shader. The AMBIENT_LIGHT is already multiplied by the albedo when we receive it, while I would have expected it to just be the "sum" of the ambient light. This leads to this render : While I was expecting this : I corrected the issue on our version of the engine to get the second image. You can check my changes here : https://github.com/godotengine/godot/commit/3cdd6f6dec8cd20991dc5ace555dbc7ab14cfca0 The key is to "freeze" the value of ambient light before it is multiplied by the albedo (around line 2150 in scene_forward_clustered.glsl for instance). I haven't tested it on the test project you provided, but it works exactly like we expect for us.

This is on some level understandable, but it is very strange to argue that the compatibility renderer should be a blocker for implementing new rendering features in the advanced renderers. I would believe that the inherent point of using the compatibility renderer is that the user does not intend to implement advanced graphics effects, and thus will likely not be surprised that certain features are unsupported by their renderer.

Those affected would be free to [open an issue in godot-proposals](https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues), or consider implementing support for the feature themselves.

Some features definitely can't be supported on compatibility. For those, we do diverge.

This one needs to be investigated before diverging.

Cel shading for compatibility render seems very reasonable considering the usecases for the compatibility renderer.

>

>

Okay, but what's the timeline here? Who's responsible for it? Is it worth waiting for however long they take to finish implementing it? If it's such a simple feature and a short wait that the compatibility renderer should reasonably have it, why not just put this behind a simple console warning and allow for the compatibility renderer to catch up to the other renderers in whatever brief time it takes for it to catch up?

I see a feature that's implemented and demonstrably works now, and I see an entry on a vague todo list that's not progressing in years. Which one are we sticking to?

The solution for this that's the most likely to be merged is shader templates. (See: https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/94427 )

> Okay, but what's the timeline here? Who's responsible for it? Is it worth waiting for however long they take to finish implementing it? If it's such a simple feature and a short wait that the compatibility renderer should reasonably have it, why not just put this behind a simple console warning and allow for the compatibility renderer to catch up to the other renderers in whatever brief time it takes for it to catch up?

I've already said that we don't want to diverge unless strictly necessary. And no, it's not simple. There's no good solution for GLES3 that doesn't either imply big maintainance cost (having the option for single pass lighting) or big performance cost (having single pass lighting for everything) or shaders that are broken from one backend to the other (this PR). So we'd be shipping something that will stay broken in gles3.

As the original OP of the proposal this addresses 6 years ago, believe me i understand the frustration. I am frustrated too. But if there's priorities in how we design and ship the engine, then we need to find a way to work with them, and shader templates is the current way forward.
